title: Organize, Develop & Revise - Transfer Check
description: A second source pair for applying organization, development, revision, and editing skills beyond the core focused module.
subject: rla
passage:
Source A: Extend the Learning Center to 9 p.m.

The community college should keep its Learning Center open until 9 p.m. Monday through Thursday. In a spring survey of 640 students, 38 percent of respondents said work or caregiving made it difficult to use tutoring before 5 p.m. During a four-week pilot, the center stayed open three extra hours on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Evening sessions averaged 31 student visits, and 72 percent of those visitors had not used the center during daytime hours that week. The pilot required one tutor and one front-desk employee per evening. Because the center already pays utilities until 10 p.m. for nearby classrooms, facilities staff estimated that the main added cost would be wages. Evening hours would not solve every scheduling problem, but the pilot suggests that later access reaches students who are currently underrepresented in tutoring.

Source B: Expand Asynchronous Academic Help Instead

The college should put new tutoring funds into an online question-and-response service rather than longer building hours. Students could submit questions at any time, and tutors could answer them during scheduled shifts. This approach would help students whose work schedules change from week to week and students who commute long distances. The spring survey found that 54 percent of respondents wanted “more online academic support,” a larger share than the 38 percent reporting difficulty with the current tutoring schedule. Online support would also create a written record students could review later. The college has not yet run a full asynchronous tutoring pilot, so the number of students who would use it and the average response time are unknown. A small trial in two math courses received 86 questions in three weeks, but participation varied sharply by instructor. The service may offer broader access, yet the college would need clearer evidence about staffing, response quality, and demand before treating it as a complete replacement for evening tutoring.

questions.prompt: Which outline provides the clearest progression for an essay arguing that Source A is better supported?
questions.explanation: The outline establishes the judgment early, organizes evidence by evaluative reasons, compares the weaker source, and preserves qualification.
questions.rule: Organize an ER around reasons for your judgment, not around separate source summaries.

options.text: Summarize Source A -> summarize Source B -> state a preference in the conclusion.
options.whyWrong: This structure reports content but postpones the evaluation and does not organize around reasons.

options.text: State the evaluation -> analyze Source A’s pilot evidence -> compare Source B’s untested assumptions -> acknowledge what Source A still does not prove.
List every number from both sources -> discuss commuting -> repeat the thesis.
options.whyWrong: The evidence is not organized by a clear evaluative purpose.

options.text: Describe personal experiences with tutoring -> summarize the survey -> choose a source.
options.whyWrong: Personal experience does not replace analysis of the supplied arguments.

questions.prompt: Which transition best completes the comparison? “Source A has direct pilot evidence about evening users. ___, Source B has not tested its service at college-wide scale.”
questions.explanation: “By contrast” accurately signals the shift from tested pilot evidence to an untested broader proposal.
questions.rule: Choose transitions for the logical relationship, not because they sound formal.

options.text: For example
options.whyWrong: The second sentence is not an example of Source A’s evidence.

options.text: As a result
options.whyWrong: Source A’s pilot did not cause Source B to lack a pilot.

options.text: In the same way
options.whyWrong: The sentences emphasize a difference in evidence strength.

options.text: By contrast

questions.prompt: Which sentence best develops the claim that Source A has stronger evidence about actual use?
questions.explanation: The sentence explains the significance of the pilot statistic and connects it directly to the argument being evaluated.
questions.rule: After evidence, explain what it proves and why that matters to your thesis.

options.text: The 72 percent figure matters because it shows the pilot reached many students who had not used daytime tutoring that week, directly connecting the trial to Source A’s access claim.
Source A says 72 percent, which is a large number.
options.whyWrong: This repeats the statistic without explaining what it demonstrates.

options.text: Tutoring is important because students need help.
options.whyWrong: The statement is generic and not tied to the source evidence.

options.text: Source B mentions 54 percent, so Source A must be correct.
options.whyWrong: A different survey percentage does not automatically validate Source A.

questions.prompt: A paragraph already explains that Source B’s 54 percent survey result shows interest in online support. Which sentence would best deepen the analysis?
questions.explanation: This addition identifies what the evidence measures, its limitation, and how that affects the comparison between sources.
questions.rule: Depth comes from interpreting the limits and significance of evidence.

options.text: Online services are common today.
options.whyWrong: The statement adds no source-based analysis.

options.text: Fifty-four percent is more than half.
options.whyWrong: This restates the number without evaluating it.

options.text: However, the survey measures interest rather than actual repeated use, so it is weaker evidence for how the proposed service would perform than Source A’s completed pilot is for evening attendance.
The college should always choose the option preferred by the largest percentage of students.
options.whyWrong: The essay must evaluate evidence and tradeoffs, not apply an unsupported rule.

questions.prompt: Which revision makes this sentence more focused? “Source A is stronger because it has a pilot, the college has many classrooms, tutoring can be stressful, and the pilot provides actual attendance data.”
questions.explanation: The revision removes unrelated classroom and stress details while preserving the evidence-based reason for the judgment.
questions.rule: Cut any detail that does not help prove the paragraph’s specific point.

options.text: Source A is stronger because it has a pilot, the college has many classrooms, tutoring can sometimes be stressful for some students, and the pilot provides actual attendance data.
options.whyWrong: The revision keeps the unrelated material and adds words without improving focus.

options.text: Source A is stronger because tutoring exists.
options.whyWrong: This removes the evidence that supports the comparison.

options.text: The college has many classrooms, and Source A is stronger.
options.whyWrong: The revision keeps an irrelevant fact and drops the useful reason.

options.text: Source A is stronger because its pilot provides actual attendance data about the proposed evening hours.

questions.prompt: Which revision improves clarity and logical order most? “Source B might reach commuters. Its college-wide demand is unknown. Therefore, the proposal could improve access, but the evidence is less direct than Source A’s pilot.”
questions.explanation: The revision places the potential benefit beside its evidence limitation and then states the comparison clearly.
questions.rule: Clarity improves when evidence, limitation, and evaluation appear in a logical sequence.

options.text: Source B might reach commuters. Therefore, Source A ran a pilot. Its college-wide demand is unknown.
options.whyWrong: The transition creates a false logical connection.

options.text: Source B could improve access for commuters, but its college-wide demand is still unknown; therefore, that benefit is less directly supported than Source A’s pilot-based access claim is.
College-wide demand is unknown. Commuters exist. Source B has a proposal.
options.whyWrong: The sentences become less connected and the evaluation is obscured.

options.text: Source B is less direct, and commuters might be reached, and demand is unknown, and Source A has a pilot.
options.whyWrong: The sentence is harder to follow because it strings several ideas together without clear relationships.

questions.prompt: Which revision best corrects the sentence without changing its meaning? “Source A provide attendance data from a pilot, while Source B have only a limited course trial.”
questions.explanation: The revision fixes subject-verb agreement and keeps the comparison in one correctly punctuated sentence.
questions.rule: In final editing, protect meaning while fixing the specific convention error.

options.text: Source A providing attendance data from a pilot, while Source B having only a limited course trial.
options.whyWrong: This creates a fragment without finite verbs.

options.text: Source A provide attendance data from a pilot; while Source B has only a limited course trial.
options.whyWrong: “Provide” still disagrees with the singular subject, and the semicolon before “while” is incorrect here.

options.text: Source A provides attendance data from a pilot, while Source B has only a limited course trial.
Source A provides attendance data, from a pilot while Source B, has only a limited course trial.
options.whyWrong: The added commas interrupt the sentence incorrectly.

questions.prompt: Which sentence most needs revision for Standard English?
questions.explanation: Option A has a subject-verb agreement error: the singular subject “evidence” requires “does not show.”
questions.rule: Look for convention errors that interfere with clarity before making optional style changes.

options.text: Although Source B offers flexible access, its evidence do not show how consistently students would use the service.
Source A’s pilot lasted four weeks, so a longer trial could provide more reliable evidence.
options.whyWrong: This sentence uses standard agreement and punctuation.

options.text: The two sources address the same access problem but support different solutions.
options.whyWrong: This sentence is complete and correctly structured.

options.text: Because Source A reports actual attendance, its evidence is more direct for the proposed schedule.
options.whyWrong: The introductory clause and main clause are correctly formed.

curriculum.learningObjective: Transfer organization, development, revision, and conventions skills to a new paired-source context.
